description: The five pillars of the PlexusOne platform, rendered on the homepage and the pillar pages. Order follows the build -> run -> ship story, then the specs underneath and the workbench. Every repo listed here must be public.

pillars.name: Agents
pillars.tagline: Production AI agents in Go, built from composable Omni modules.
pillars.outcome: AI agents and the Omni modules for models, voice, chat, search, memory, and skills.
pillars.description: OmniAgent is the agent framework at the center of this family. It is assembled from single-purpose Omni modules: each one puts a provider-neutral Go interface in front of one capability, such as LLMs, voice, chat, search, or secrets. Use the whole stack or import one module into your own code.

highlights.title: Provider-neutral by design
highlights.description: Switch LLM, voice, search, or observability vendors without changing application code.

highlights.title: Multi-channel experiences
highlights.description: The same agent can answer over chat, SMS, voice calls, or a live meeting.

highlights.title: Skills, memory, and tools
highlights.description: Reusable skills, long-term memory, MCP tools, and browser automation for agents.

highlights.title: Agent teams
highlights.description: Define multi-agent teams once in Multi-Agent Spec and generate plugins for AI coding assistants.

highlights.title: Evaluation built in
highlights.description: LLM-as-judge reports and observability hooks to measure agents, not just run them.

highlights.title: Small, independent modules
highlights.description: Each module does one job and stays usable without the framework.

pillars.name: Systems
pillars.tagline: The SaaS backbone: identity, tenancy, connections, and billing for Go.
pillars.outcome: Multi-tenant SaaS backends with SystemForge: identity, tenancy, connections, keys, and billing.
pillars.description: SystemForge is a batteries-included Go platform module for multi-tenant SaaS: Django- and Laravel-style conveniences for Go. It gives every app the same sign-in, sessions, authorization, and tenant isolation, whether you run one monolith or many services. SystemForge Web supplies the React front end, and ConnectForge, KeyForge, and PayForge handle connections, keys, and billing.

highlights.title: Built-in OAuth 2.0 / OIDC server
highlights.description: SystemAuth runs standalone or embedded. Authorization Code + PKCE, client credentials, refresh rotation with reuse detection, and DPoP.

highlights.title: Tenant isolation in the database
highlights.description: PostgreSQL row-level security, with organizations, memberships, and per-organization feature flags.

highlights.title: Fine-grained authorization
highlights.description: RBAC and relationship-based access control through a Zanzibar-style provider and HTTP middleware.

highlights.title: Monolith or microservices
highlights.description: Host many apps in one server, with a schema and database login per app, or federate separate services to one sign-in.

highlights.title: Enterprise-ready identity
highlights.description: Social login, SCIM 2.0 provisioning, invite-only sign-up, and OCSF security events for your SIEM.

highlights.title: Billing from a pricing spec
highlights.description: PayForge turns a SystemSpec pricing definition into a product catalog, checkout, and entitlements.

pillars.name: Operations
pillars.tagline: Keep hundreds of repositories released, patched, and compliant.
pillars.outcome: Policy-driven automation for dependency updates, releases, and CI/CD across GitHub organizations.
pillars.description: When you ship a SaaS product from many repositories, upkeep becomes the bottleneck. VersionConductor and PipelineConductor apply Cedar policy-as-code across GitHub organizations: one merges dependency updates and cuts maintenance releases, the other keeps CI/CD pipelines consistent and reports where they drift.

highlights.title: Organization-wide

highlights.title: Safe by default
highlights.description: Dry-run unless you pass --execute. Merge profiles range from aggressive to a five-day quarantine.

highlights.title: Reports your tools understand

highlights.title: Runs in CI

pillars.name: Specs
pillars.tagline: Open, machine-readable specs that agents and tools can act on.
pillars.outcome: SystemSpec and agent specs: architecture, design, APIs, pricing, and deployment as machine-readable definitions that drive generation, linting, and review.
pillars.description: Every layer of the platform is described by an open specification. The SystemSpec family covers the parts of a software system: architecture, design system, API style, pricing and packaging, and deployment topology. Multi-Agent Spec and Structured Evaluation do the same for agent teams and their evaluation. Each spec is Go-first with a generated JSON Schema, so one definition can produce documentation, linters, diagrams, LLM rubrics, and instructions for AI agents.

highlights.title: One source, many outputs
highlights.description: Generate docs, deterministic lint rules, diagrams, LLM rubrics, and agent instructions from one definition.

highlights.title: Built for AI agents
highlights.description: MCP servers and generated context let coding agents follow the spec and review work against it.

highlights.title: CI gates
highlights.description: Validate and diff specs in CI: security readiness, design violations, API conformance levels.

highlights.title: Go-first schemas
highlights.description: Go types are the source of truth; JSON Schemas are generated from them, never hand-written.

highlights.title: Specs drive runtimes
highlights.description: PayForge bills from the pricing spec; agent teams deploy from Multi-Agent Spec.

pillars.name: PlexusOne App
pillars.tagline: A native macOS workbench for running many AI coding agents at once.
pillars.outcome: The macOS workbench where we build all of the above: many Claude Code sessions in one grid, tracked, alerted, and restored after a crash.
pillars.description: PlexusOne Desktop runs AI coding agents such as Claude Code side by side in a grid of terminal panes, backed by your own tmux sessions. It tracks every Claude Code session — its name, live status, the repositories it touched, and its cost — alerts you when one is waiting for you, and restores everything in one step after a crash or restart. It's a native Swift app, and it's how the rest of PlexusOne gets built.

highlights.title: Many agents, one grid
highlights.description: Panes from 1×1 to 4×4 across multiple windows, with keyboard navigation between them.

highlights.title: Claude Sessions window
highlights.description: Every session with its subject, repositories, last prompt, cost, and how it ended.

highlights.title: One-step crash recovery
highlights.description: Recreates missing tmux sessions and resumes each Claude session where it left off.

highlights.title: Waiting alerts
highlights.description: A notification and Dock badge when a session waits at a prompt; ⌘J jumps to it.

highlights.title: Live status in every pane
highlights.description: Claude session names plus busy, idle, or waiting status in each pane header.

highlights.title: Next: agents that talk to each other
highlights.description: Communication between agent sessions, building on AgentPair, is on the roadmap.
